method: symmetric four-world authoring, post-hoc seeded key selection

items.setting: A town cobbler counter; the cobbler is speaking to a customer who left a pair of boots

worlds.line: Your boots are done early — the new soles went on smoothly.
worlds.reply: I'll collect them now, then — ahead of schedule suits me.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The cobbler reports finished work, so collecting the boots on the spot is the natural next move. Hunting for a replacement pair contradicts a repair that already succeeded. Promising to drop off a second boot tomorrow assumes work hasn't started, and naming rubber soles is too late once the soles are fitted.

kills.1: "the new soles" are already fitted, so the boots were saved; shopping for a replacement pair answers a repair that never failed.
kills.2: "done early" means the job is finished, so there is nothing left to deliver to the bench tomorrow morning.
kills.3: the soles "went on smoothly" already, so choosing a sole material now would be a decision made after the fact.

worlds.line: The heel cracked right through, so these boots can't be resoled.
worlds.reply: I'll start looking for a replacement pair this week, then.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The cobbler declares the boots unrepairable, so accepting that and planning to buy another pair is the fitting response. Collecting finished boots is impossible when nothing was repaired. Offering to bring in a matching boot assumes work is about to begin, and picking a sole material assumes the repair is going ahead.

kills.0: if they "can't be resoled" there is no completed repair waiting at the counter to be taken away.
kills.2: the heel "cracked right through", so no job is being prepared and no second boot is needed at the bench.
kills.3: "so these boots" are being written off entirely, which makes a choice between sole materials pointless.

worlds.line: Could you bring the matching left boot in before I start?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The cobbler asks for the second boot, so agreeing and naming a delivery time is the cooperative answer. Nothing is finished, so collecting a repair makes no sense. The boots are treated as repairable, which rules out shopping for replacements, and no material question has been put to the customer.
worlds.reply: It's at home; I'll drop it off tomorrow morning.

kills.0: the work is still "before I start", so there is no completed pair to pick up this evening.
kills.1: asking for "the matching left boot" shows the repair is going forward, so abandoning the boots for a new pair misreads it.
kills.3: the request is "before I start" for a missing boot, not a question about which sole material to use.

worlds.line: Do you want rubber soles or leather ones on these?
worlds.reply: Rubber, please — I walk on wet pavement most days.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The cobbler poses a straight choice, so naming one material with a reason answers it. Nothing has been finished yet, so collecting the boots is premature. The boots are clearly being resoled, so writing them off is wrong, and no second boot has been asked for.

kills.0: the choice of "rubber soles or leather" is still open, so the boots cannot already be waiting for collection.
kills.1: offering "or leather ones" shows the boots are repairable, so giving up and buying another pair does not follow.
kills.2: "rubber soles or leather" is a question about material, not a request for a missing boot to be brought in.

items.setting: An independent bookshop orders desk; the bookseller is speaking to a customer about a special order

worlds.line: Special orders from that publisher usually take about a month.
worlds.reply: A month is fine — I'll wait rather than order online.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The bookseller gives a plain lead time, so accepting that wait is the natural reply. No format mix-up has been raised, so correcting paperback to hardcover answers nothing. No holding period has been proposed, and the book has plainly not arrived yet.

kills.1: a line that only says orders "take about a month" makes no claim about paperback or hardcover to correct.
kills.2: "about a month" is a delivery estimate, not an offer to keep a copy behind the counter for two weeks.
kills.3: orders that "usually take about" a month have not landed, so nothing can be carried out of the shop today.

worlds.line: You ordered the paperback, but I've written down hardcover here.
worlds.reply: Paperback is right — please change the record before it ships.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The bookseller flags a mismatch in the order record, so confirming which format is correct is what's needed. No timeline has been quoted, so agreeing to a month-long wait is unmoored. Nothing has been offered about holding a copy, and the order isn't even correct yet, let alone arrived.

kills.0: having "written down hardcover" is a record problem; no delivery estimate was given for a customer to accept.
kills.2: "You ordered the paperback" raises a format error, not any arrangement to hold a copy for two weeks.
kills.3: since "I've written down hardcover", the order is still being fixed and no copy is sitting ready to take home.

worlds.keyAct: accepts the hold and sets a pickup day
worlds.line: Once it comes in, I can hold it for two weeks.
worlds.reply: Two weeks is plenty; I'll collect it on Saturday morning.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The bookseller offers a holding window, so accepting it and naming a collection day fits. No lead time has been quoted, so a month-long wait has nothing to attach to. No format was disputed, and the book is explicitly not in yet.

kills.0: "Once it comes in" states a condition, not an estimate, so there is no month-long wait being accepted.
kills.1: an offer to "hold it for two weeks" says nothing about paperback or hardcover being recorded wrongly.
kills.3: the copy is still only expected "Once it comes in", so it cannot already be in the shop to carry away.

worlds.line: Your copy arrived this morning, a full week ahead of schedule.
worlds.reply: I'll take it with me now, since it's already in.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The bookseller announces an early arrival, so leaving with the book is the natural response. Accepting a month-long wait contradicts a book that is already here. No format error was mentioned, and no two-week holding period was proposed.

kills.0: a copy that "arrived this morning" has already come, so agreeing to wait a month for it makes no sense.
kills.1: "Your copy arrived" is an arrival announcement with nothing said about paperback versus hardcover.
kills.2: since it "arrived this morning" and is being handed over, no two-week hold was ever put on the table.

worlds.line: Your light meter tested fine — the readings match my reference exactly.
worlds.reply: That saves a repair bill; I'll keep shooting with it.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The technician reports a clean test, so deciding to carry on using the camera follows naturally. Promising to bring a strap answers a request that wasn't made. No trade was offered, and no battery problem was raised.

kills.1: "the readings match" a reference is a test result; nobody asked for an original strap to be brought in.
kills.2: "Your light meter tested fine" is a diagnosis, not an offer of store credit for the camera.
kills.3: readings that "match my reference exactly" say nothing about batteries being out of production.

worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The technician asks for a missing accessory, so saying where it is and when it will arrive is the cooperative answer. A clean meter result was never reported. No credit was offered, and no battery issue was mentioned.

kills.0: "the original strap" is what's being requested; no light-meter test result has been reported at all.
kills.2: since pricing waits "so I can price it", no store credit has been offered for anything yet.
kills.3: a request to "bring the original strap" concerns an accessory, not discontinued batteries.

kills.1: the offer is "for this body" as it stands, with no missing strap asked for.

kills.0: a warning that the model "takes a battery" no longer made is not a report of accurate meter readings.

items.setting: A visitor and the attendant at the local museum cloakroom

worlds.line: Could you hold my rucksack until the last tour finishes?
worlds.reply: Take tag forty-one; we keep bags until half five.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: A bag is being handed in for the afternoon, so giving a tag and the closing time completes the transaction. Asking for a description of a coat needs a lost ticket, which was not mentioned. Pointing at the pushchair alcove answers a different question, and fetching a wooden-handled umbrella responds to a mix-up nobody reported.

kills.1: I am asking you to "hold my rucksack" now; nothing of mine was washed, so being asked to describe a coat fits nothing.
kills.2: Handing over a rucksack until "the last tour" ends is not a question about where a pushchair may go.
kills.3: I want my rucksack kept until "the last tour" finishes; I have not been handed the wrong umbrella.

worlds.line: The ticket for my coat went through the wash yesterday.
worlds.reply: Describe the coat and I'll look along the rail.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The claim ticket is destroyed, so asking for a description and offering to search the rail is the way to recover the coat. Issuing a tag needs a bag being handed in, not one already stored. Directing pushchairs to an alcove answers another question, and fetching a wooden-handled umbrella addresses a swap nobody described.

kills.0: My coat is already with you and "The ticket" is ruined; there is no bag to tag and take in.
kills.2: Losing a ticket "through the wash" is not a question about leaving a pushchair anywhere.
kills.3: I have lost "The ticket" for a coat, not been handed somebody else's umbrella.

worlds.line: Is there anywhere to leave a folded pushchair down here?
worlds.reply: The alcove behind me takes pushchairs and walking frames.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The visitor asks where bulky items go, so naming the alcove that takes them answers it directly. Issuing a bag tag with a closing time responds to a bag handed over, not a question about space. Asking for a coat description needs a lost ticket, and producing a wooden-handled umbrella addresses a mix-up nobody raised.

kills.0: I asked where "a folded pushchair" can go, not to have a bag tagged and held for me.
kills.1: Nothing of mine is lost; asking about "a folded pushchair" gives you no coat to search the rail for.
kills.3: My question is about space "down here" for a pushchair, not about being given the wrong umbrella.

worlds.line: That's not my umbrella — mine has a wooden handle.
worlds.reply: The wooden-handled one is further along; I'll bring it.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The wrong umbrella has been handed over, so locating the right one and fetching it corrects the mistake. Giving a bag tag responds to something being handed in, not taken back. Asking for a coat description belongs to a lost ticket, and pointing out the pushchair alcove answers a question that was not asked.

kills.0: I am refusing an umbrella that is "not my umbrella"; there is no bag of mine to tag and hold.
kills.1: Saying it is "not my umbrella" concerns an umbrella, so searching the coat rail is the wrong hunt.
kills.2: Describing "a wooden handle" identifies my umbrella; it asks nothing about where pushchairs may go.

items.setting: A caller and the presenter on the community radio request line

worlds.line: Could you play something for my gran's ninetieth on Sunday?
worlds.reply: Give me her name and a song and it's yours.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: A dedication has been asked for, so requesting the name and the track and agreeing to play it grants the request. Reading out a corrected time responds to a listings error nobody pointed out. Booking a studio slot answers an offer to perform, and appealing to listeners answers a report of something missing.

kills.1: Asking you to "play something" for a birthday corrects nothing you announced, so reading out a fixed time fits nothing.
kills.2: A request for "my gran's" ninetieth is not an offer to perform, so booking me into a studio makes no sense.
kills.3: I am asking for a song for "my gran's" birthday; nothing of mine is missing for listeners to watch for.

worlds.line: You said the fair starts at ten; the poster says eleven.
worlds.reply: I'll read the corrected time out after this record.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The station gave a wrong start time, so promising to put the right one out on air is the fitting fix. Taking a name and a song belongs to a dedication that was not requested. Booking a studio slot answers an offer to play, and appealing to listeners answers a report of something lost.

kills.0: I am pointing out that "the poster says" eleven; I have asked for no dedication at all.
kills.2: Correcting when "the fair starts" is not an offer to come and perform in the studio.
kills.3: Saying "the poster says" eleven corrects a printed time; nothing is lost for listeners to look out for.

worlds.line: I could bring in my accordion for the Friday folk hour.
worlds.reply: Come at seven — we'll mic you up in studio two.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: A musician has offered to play live, so naming an arrival time and a studio accepts the offer. Asking for a name and a song belongs to a dedication that was not requested. Reading out a corrected time answers a listings error nobody raised, and appealing to listeners answers a report of something missing.

kills.0: Offering to bring "my accordion" in asks for no song to be dedicated to anyone.
kills.1: My line offers to play the "Friday folk" hour; it corrects no time you announced.
kills.3: I am offering to play "my accordion" live; no missing animal has been reported.

worlds.line: There's a lost dog wandering near the bridge on Mill Road.
worlds.reply: I'll ask listeners to look out for him after this song.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: A stray has been spotted, so putting an appeal out to listeners is what the station can usefully do. Taking a name and a track belongs to a dedication nobody requested. Reading out a corrected time answers a listings error that was not raised, and booking a studio slot answers an offer to perform.

kills.0: Reporting "a lost dog" near the bridge is not a request for a birthday dedication.
kills.1: Saying the dog is "on Mill Road" corrects no time you announced earlier.
kills.2: "a lost dog" needs finding, not an accordion slot in the studio.
